item.title: How People “Redo” Family After an Estrangement
item.description:
Family Dynamics

How People “Redo” Family After an Estrangement

New research explores how people find belonging after estrangement.

Posted September 29, 2026

How do people “redo” family after an estrangement from the family they grew up in?

This was the central question of a study by Rin Reczek of The Ohio State University. Estrangement can end more than relationships: It can disrupt holiday traditions, connections with extended family, and a person’s sense of belonging. With all of that taken together, there can be a strong need to create an alternative family.

To explore how people reestablish a family network, Reczek recruited participants through news articles mentioning the study and a post on a Reddit forum for estranged people. In the final tally, they interviewed 68 adults who were estranged from at least one member of their family of origin. Participants were, on average, 38 years old and had been estranged for 7.51 years. Reczek asked about their experiences of estrangement and how their ideas about family had changed, then analyzed their narratives for themes.

What did Reczek find? Many participants redefined family by placing greater weight on choice than on biology. One participant expressed: “Just because you’re biologically related to them doesn't mean you have any obligation to them ... And just the fact that we're related doesn't mean that I really feel anything toward you.”

A second, less common shift involved finding a sense of family through symbolic connections with deceased ancestors. This theme surfaced for five participants, all of whom were Black or Native American. One interviewee reflected: “This is a little bit more metaphysical, but I really feel a deep connection to a couple of specific ancestors on each of my sides…One of them is my grandfather... And then the other one is my maternal great-grandmother.”

Participants also changed who they counted as family and what they expected those relationships to provide. Reczek identified three ways they did this.

First, participants built safe and trustworthy relationships with friends, housemates, community members, and their own children. This theme was especially salient for LGBTQ participants. One interviewee remarked: “I never really had trust in my family. They've never been those people…my friends—I trust them ... which in my mind feels like what family should be.”

Second, some participants found parental support in surrogate relationships with older coworkers, community members, and friends’ parents. These elders offered one-way, unconditional support that the interviewees hadn't received from their parents. As one participant put it: “I now feel like I have a pseudo mom. ... She's not a perfect pseudo mom ... but it's like one of the most beautiful things I've experienced.”

Third, some participants strengthened relationships with extended relatives with whom they had remained in contact. Although estrangement from one family member can destabilize other family ties, these participants preserved parts of their kinship network by keeping up with selected relatives. One interviewee explained: “I'm the one visiting great-aunt so-and-so, great-uncle so-and-so. I'm gonna show up at all the cousins' [children's] christenings, and this and that and the other. I'll go to everything.”

The findings of this study suggest that estrangement doesn’t have to leave only an emotional void. By reframing what makes someone family, participants found relationships in which they felt safe and belonged. In other words, they redid family.

item.title: Moving From Suicidal Ideation to Liberation
item.description:
Suicide

Moving From Suicidal Ideation to Liberation

How existential psychotherapy can reframe the search for agency and hope.

Posted September 29, 2026

Key points
  • Suicidal ideation can be traced to existential concerns about meaning, isolation, freedom, and death.
  • Insights from existential psychotherapy can help restore hope and a sense of agency.
  • Existential enlightenment can be a protective factor against suicidal ideation.
Source: Mikhail Nilov / Pexels

Have you ever found yourself in a challenging situation you'd do anything to escape? Maybe you were stuck in a boring meeting or tasked with something that felt like pulling teeth. Let’s dial up the discomfort: Have you ever faced an inescapable challenge? Maybe you live with an incurable illness or are surviving the death of a loved one. In these cases, and often devastatingly, you can't reverse circumstances.

Research shows that when individuals feel stuck in life, they are at greater risk of experiencing an existential crisis: dread about the nature of our existence as humans. In turn, this state of crisis can increase one’s risk of suicidal ideation. From a philosophical perspective, liberation from crisis depends on our relationship with “the four ultimate concerns of life”, as defined by Irvin D. Yalom: death, freedom, isolation, and meaninglessness.

I like to imagine these ultimate concerns of life as pillars. As such, I invite you to imagine a home supported by them. When the pillars have a strong foundation, they are resilient enough to withstand storms and sunshine all the same. However, if even one pillar is weakened, the entire house is at risk of crumbling. Now, imagine you are that home, and consider how ideation may arise and subside depending on how we bolster your life.

What Is Suicidal Ideation, Really?

Source: Liza Summer / Pexels

Among mental health professionals, suicidal ideation is generally observed as either “passive” or “active.” Passive ideation may present as one’s desire to stop feeling emotional pain, which may involve thoughts of vanishing or ceasing to exist. With greater immediate risk, active ideation is defined by specific thoughts of ending one’s own life, which usually includes a plan for suicide or previous attempts.

With passive ideation, the individual focuses less on the details of how they would leave their earthly experience, unlike active suicidal ideation. Whether someone is experiencing active or passive ideation, the common thread is a desire to be liberated from suffering, especially existential crisis. In this state, fortifying one’s inner home as above might feel impossible.

An Existential Lens

If you ever find yourself asking questions such as “why are we really here?” and “what’s it all about?”, you are pondering the nature of human existence, and you are talking about existentialism. In the therapy room, existential psychotherapy can help us understand suicidal ideation at its base. Specifically, while death gives life meaning, thoughts of ending one’s own life can arise when life feels void of meaning, freedom, and connection.

Source: Ozan Tabakoğlu / Pexels

For instance, a sense of meaninglessness may arise from feeling misaligned with your purpose, goals, and values. Meaninglessness might intensify if you feel you lack personal freedom and, as a result, you don’t practice creativity or gratitude. When you feel you lack freedom, you are also less likely to seek healthy relationships with others or nurture a healthy relationship with yourself. We call this downward spiral “existential dread.”

In contrast, you might feel your life has meaning when living in alignment with your purpose, goals, and values. In turn, meaning can grow when you exercise your freedom of thought to be creative, innovative, and grateful. Your sense of freedom is likely to be supported when you have a healthy relationship with yourself and, of course, with others. Finally, this brings us back to meaning, since our connections must be meaningful to feel truly fulfilled. We call this upward spiral “existential enlightenment.”

Both modern and historical research on existential psychotherapy supports that one’s awareness of and care for these four pillars of life can help restore a sense of agency and hope in their lives, and most importantly, protect against suicidal ideation.

From Dread to Enlightenment

As a psychotherapist and a human being myself, I’ve learned that the desire to be liberated from suffering is often driven by two opposing forces: death or more life. The former ends life’s beauty along with the suffering, but the latter offers hope to move through suffering and enjoy some of the beauty along the way.

Source: Thirdman / Pexels

I invite you now to take a moment and reflect on someone who previously felt stuck in challenging circumstances but made meaning of their grief and sorrow; they exercised their freedom to connect with loved ones and maybe even strangers on the good, the bad, and the ugly; they referenced mortality as a way to feel grateful for the moments they have left to live out this one and precious life, and slowly but surely, they experienced some enlightenment. Maybe this was you, or maybe it will be.

When life feels too heavy, and without hope of reinforcements, it makes sense that suicidal ideation can arise. Yet, as with any challenging emotion, I’d like to validate the ideation without endorsing it; quite the opposite, in fact. By bravely pivoting from existential dread to existential enlightenment, one can take steps toward liberating themselves from intense psychological distress. Rather than saying “no” to life, you deserve to say “yes” to one where you get to come home to yourself, a home built strongly on meaning, connection, freedom, and peace with mortality.

If you or someone you love is contemplating suicide, seek help immediately. For help 24/7, dial 988 for the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline, or reach out to the Crisis Text Line by texting TALK to 741741. To find a therapist near you, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

item.title: Two Questions We Must Ask About Dementia Right Now
item.description:
Dementia

Two Questions We Must Ask About Dementia Right Now

We must support today's caregivers while protecting our own choices for tomorrow.

Posted September 29, 2026

Key points
  • Dementia caregivers need practical help, respite, education, and a dependable circle of support.
  • Caregiving should never require one person to sacrifice their health, livelihood, and identity.
  • Dementia planning must begin while we can clearly communicate and document our wishes.
  • Specific advance-care conversations protect dignity and keep families from having to guess.

After more than two decades working in hospice and end-of-life care, I can say that caring for someone living with dementia can be one of the most intense caregiving experiences a family will ever face.

The journey may continue for years. It can affect a caregiver physically, emotionally, psychologically, spiritually, and financially. As the disease progresses, families may experience repeated losses while the person they love is still physically present. Roles and relationships change. Sleep, work, finances, health, and family dynamics can all be affected.

Yet we continue to treat dementia caregiving as though one family member should somehow be able to manage it all. That is impossible. They cannot, and they should never be expected to.

At the same time, many of us have not clearly documented what we would want if we developed dementia. We may have a basic advance directive, but do we have a dementia advance directive?

When we discuss the growing dementia crisis, I believe we must focus on two urgent questions:

  1. How do we support the people caring for loved ones with dementia right now?
  2. How do we protect our own wishes if we develop dementia in the future?

Question One: How Do We Support Dementia Caregivers Today?

The first step is understanding that dementia is not one single disease. It is an umbrella term describing symptoms that affect memory, reasoning, communication, behavior, and a person's ability to perform everyday activities. Alzheimer's disease is the most common cause, but there are several other forms of dementia, each with its own progression and challenges.

Dementia also affects far more than memory. A person may experience changes in judgment, personality, sleep, mobility, appetite, language, impulse control, and the ability to recognize familiar people or surroundings. They may become anxious, frightened, agitated, withdrawn, or resistant.

When caregivers understand what may be happening beneath the behavior, they can respond with greater skill and compassion. But education alone is not enough. Even the most loving and well-informed caregiver cannot provide safe, sustainable, around-the-clock care indefinitely without meaningful support.

No One Can Caregive Alone

We need to stop letting one person do the care until they collapse. Caregiving should not require a person to neglect their own medical needs. This past August, Dolly Parton shared how she neglected her own health while caring full-time for her beloved husband.

Telling a caregiver to "take care of yourself" is not helpful if no one is available to stay with their loved one while they rest. Caregivers need tangible support. That may include:

  • Regular respite care
  • Help with meals, errands, transportation, and household tasks
  • A share calendar that allows family and friends to choose specific ways to help
  • Education about the disease process and what changes to expect
  • Support groups and opportunities to speak honestly without judgment
  • Home-safety evaluations
  • Financial and legal guidance
  • Adult day programs or professional in-home assistance
  • Access to hospice or palliative care when medically appropriate
  • A plan for emergencies and caregiver illness

Most importantly, caregiving must become a shared responsibility. Families, friends, neighbors, faith communities, healthcare organizations, and local communities all have a role to play. Instead of asking a caregiver, “Let me know if you need anything,” we can offer something specific, such as:

  • “I can stay with your mother every Tuesday from 2 to 5.”
  • “I’m bringing dinner on Thursday.”
  • “I can take care of the grocery shopping this week.”
  • “I will make the phone calls and research respite services.”
  • “I can sit with you while we complete the paperwork.”

Small, dependable acts of service can become a lifeline.

Question Two: How Do We Protect Our Own Wishes for the Future?

The second question is more difficult, but it is equally urgent: What would we want if we developed dementia?

Most people say they do not want to live for years without awareness, meaningful connection, or what they personally consider an acceptable quality of life.

Planning Must Begin Before a Crisis

Dementia planning must happen while a person still has the capacity to understand their choices, communicate preferences, and complete the appropriate documents.

A strong plan should include a dementia advance directive and thoughtful conversations about the realities of progressive cognitive decline. Consider taking the following steps:

  1. Define quality of life in your own words. Be specific about the abilities, relationships, experiences, and level of awareness that make life meaningful to you.
  2. Put your wishes in writing and even make a video of you sharing them and explaining why you are making the choices you are.
  3. Talk openly with your family. Documents are important, but conversations help loved ones understand the thinking and values behind your decisions.

None of us knows what we will be like as we age, but longer lifespans usually mean we will face physical, cognitive, and/or financial challenges. Planning ahead gives both you and your family a road map.

This Is About Practical Compassionate Planning, Not Fear

Talking about dementia planning is not giving up on life. It is a choice. A social worker I know said that the most common question she gets from dementia caregivers is: "How do I ensure I do not end up in this suspended place, with no quality of life?"

This conversation is about respecting a person's individual, subjective, informed choice. It is about recognizing that dignity and quality of life are personal. It is about supporting people who are living with dementia today while allowing all of us to express what we would want if we ourselves got a dementia diagnosis tomorrow.

item.title: Why Can’t We Be Friends? Resolving Sibling Rivalry
item.description:
Family Dynamics

Why Can’t We Be Friends? Resolving Sibling Rivalry

Brothers fight with brothers, sisters with sisters. Why? What can be done?

Posted September 29, 2026

“Two children fighting over a piece of bread” (1803-1809) by Henri-Pierre Danloux (1753-1809)
Source: Sotheby’s Paris / Public Domain

When our youngest daughter was born, as a conscientious parent intent on preventing sibling rivalry, I took the advice of a pediatric expert and bought an inflatable Bozo the Clown bop bag toy, an inflatable clown that stood almost as high as our two-year-old. The expert had warned that the first-born might feel displaced by the new baby and jealousy could follow. Bozo the Clown would be our elder daughter’s punching bag, a way for her to safely express her aggressive feelings. Here’s what happened. She eyed Bozo, with his goofy wide smile and orange hair, and ran away terrified. This isn’t to say she didn’t have jealous feelings. Rivalrous feelings can take many forms; outward aggression is only one.

Rivalry between siblings is as old as humankind. As a species, we navigate between a survival instinct that favors resource competition (Darwin’s survival of the fittest) and a survival instinct for connection (Bowlby’s attachment theory1). In the animal kingdom, we can well imagine puppies scrambling for their mother’s teat and forcing out the runt. But to survive, the runt needs to remain part of the pack. We humans are not so different. The sociolinguist Deborah Tannen, in her book, You Were Always Mom’s Favorite: Sisters in Conversation Throughout Their Lives, describes how deadly instinctive impulses can be among non-human species:

“Among some bird species, second eggs are laid as back-ups, needed only if the first hatchling dies. If the first hatched chick is healthy and hale, one of its jobs when the second egg hatches is to push the newcomer out of the nest. The second chick’s death is needed to ensure the first chick’s survival.”2

Some tadpoles, sand tiger sharks, and other creatures eat their siblings.

But it’s not only food siblings fight over. Competition is a key factor in survival, and children compete for the “non-material food” of love and attention as well. From fairy tales, myths, Greek tragedies, and religious texts, the oldest stories attest that a “poverty of care” can lead to envy and bullying, even murder, among siblings.

Favoritism—extending special support or affection or preferential treatment and advantage to one member of a family—sets up a hierarchy of comparison: “the good one” versus “the bad one”; “the beautiful one” versus “the plain one.” The athletic brother, the smart daughter, the musical child versus their opposite. Parents may try to provide equal support and attention to their children, but children compete to establish their own identity within a family. Each of us wants to be perceived and acknowledged as individuals. Treating each child fairly does not necessarily make them feel special.3

Favoritism and its disastrous effects are at the heart of the well-known fairy tale of Cinderella. Her malevolent stepsisters give us the shivers. Greedy, jealous, and narcissistic, they project their feelings of inferiority onto the kind and beautiful Aschenputtel (“The Little Ash Girl” was the title of the Grimms’ version). They label Cinderella with everything they fear in themselves, their inner worthlessness, and torment and belittle her. The psychoanalyst Bruno Bettelheim argued that “the story of Cinderella resonates with children’s unconscious fears and desires related to sibling rivalry, as the protagonist’s degradation and perseverance mirror the internal struggles many children experience when they feel overshadowed by siblings."4 Tannen writes: “In families with more than one child, each additional child necessarily limits the available resources—time and attention as well as money. Limited resources make competition inevitable, and whenever there is competition, it makes sense to try to weaken or even eliminate rivals.”5

Fraternal envy and rivalry and its deadly consequences are the core of the Biblical story of Cain and Abel. Cain, the eldest, is a farmer, and brings the best of his crops as an offering to God. Abel, a shepherd, offers God the best lambs from his flock. Abel’s offerings please God, but Cain’s offerings are rejected. In revenge, Cain invites his brother into the field and kills him. God punishes Cain for the murder of his brother by condemning him to wander the earth as an exile and fugitive.

Divorce can also be a factor in creating a division among siblings. One child may become “father’s best friend” while the other child may align with her mother. The parents’ altercations and alienation from each other form the battlegrounds to which side the siblings pledge their allegiance.6

The good news is that there are now many structured programs for resolving sibling rivalry. An important first step to stop sibling aggression and abuse is for professionals and practitioners to educate themselves on the differences between normative and harmful sibling behavior. Parents may find mediation techniques helpful when dealing with sibling conflict and minor aggression. A mediational approach, however, is not appropriate when sibling abuse is present. Some parents and children may not recognize that a sibling’s behavior is abusive, so routine screenings for violent, coercive, and harmful sibling behaviors are critical.7

Human relationships are not static and unchangeable. Whatever your childhood experience or your experience as a parent refereeing sibling rivalry, it’s never too late to transform the underlying issues at the root of alienation from a brother or sister. Is now a time in your life to seek reconnection? What was your experience with your sibs? Was there rivalry? How did it manifest? Has the rivalry continued over time? What is your vision for a harmonious relationship? What has to change in your attitude or the attitude of your sibling? How can your differences be a source of wonder and joy?

item.title: Wedding Planning Offers a Glimpse Into Married Life
item.description:
Marriage

Wedding Planning Offers a Glimpse Into Married Life

Before you say "I do," change the small habits that can harm your relationship.

Posted September 29, 2026

Key points
  • The way you communicate during wedding planning can predict future conflict.
  • Catch minor issues before they grow into unsolvable conflicts.
  • Practicing appreciation and vulnerability strengthens future communication.

Planning your wedding requires communication, negotiation, decision-making, prioritizing, and budgeting, all of which will come up time and again throughout your marriage. These tasks can either connect or divide you as a couple, depending on how you manage them. The inspiration for this blog stems from my work as a wedding coordinator and couples therapist. As a wedding coordinator, I worked with couples at their happiest. As a couples therapist, I see people at their worst and sometimes most desperate. Almost every couple I see now was once that happy couple on their wedding day.

Can you see the trouble coming?

There are certainly precursors of concerning problems. It’s not always a large event that destroys relationship satisfaction. In fact, it's usually something small and more insidious, such as poor communication, repeated small misunderstandings, or failure to repair minor ruptures. The smaller things are more difficult to recognize in the moment unless you know what you're looking for. Planning your wedding provides multiple opportunities to set healthy precedents. Take it as an opportunity to identify and change small issues before they cause major conflicts.

Here are five communication strategies to use while planning your wedding and the insidious, potentially harmful habits they help prevent.

1. Listen even if you disagree.

Maybe you disagree on the budget, invite list, seating arrangements, or cake flavor. Do not skip the step of hearing your future spouse’s opinions. Listening gives the message that the other person matters. Maybe your future spouse is quiet or tends not to have very strong opinions. That’s fine; don’t force anything, but do make sure you give them the opportunity to share even a mild preference. The invitation matters in the long term. The insidious habit you are undermining here is unilateral decision-making.

2. Never stop appreciating each other's point of view.

Thank them for having the bravery to share. (You don’t literally have to say thank you.) Saying things like "I appreciate...," "I hear you," or simply using the active listening skills you learned in elementary school all serve this principle well. With the number of decisions you have to make while planning a wedding, you will have plenty of opportunities to appreciate each other's views, whether you agree or disagree. Recognize that there is vulnerability every time you share an opinion on something big or small. In a marriage, you want to encourage and reinforce vulnerability. Make it easy to share regardless of the circumstances. The insidious habit you are undermining is dismissal.

3. Share your hopes and limits for the wedding.

Don’t assume your partner knows everything you are thinking. You may both want a big wedding, but you may define this very differently. In wedding planning, there is a focal point, a shared and specific goal: getting married. It is the perfect context to practice being more specific with each other because it only gets more complicated as you build your lives. Practice clarifying. The insidious habit you are undermining is having unsaid expectations. This is important: Couples who "just grew apart” or have lots of little conflicts likely failed to share what they want, and this means that needs went unrecognized and unmet. They held their partner to a set of internal standards that were not communicated. You know each other well, but over the years you will both change. It is better to overshare. Tell your future spouse you want that outdoor wedding and why you want it.

4. Recognize tension.

A really powerful strength of committed relationships is the ability to co-regulate. However, we cannot tap into that benefit if we do not talk about emotional states. If you feel something, you need to say something. Both of you will feel busy with varying degrees of stress while planning your wedding. Don’t succumb to the false belief that your feelings are a burden to your partner. The insidious habit you are undermining here is treating your partner as fragile. When this habit expands, couples stop sharing their needs, causing resentment and unhappiness.

5. Work toward compromise.

This can only happen if you accept and invite each other's influence. To read more about accepting influence, I would point you to the Gottmans' research in their Love Lab (https://www.gottman.com/about/research/couples/). Influence is not control, and compromise is not always 50/50. You will both have priorities for your wedding day. One person may feel more strongly about being married in a hometown, and the other cares more about the menu. If you are having trouble reaching compromises, make sure you are adhering to points 1 through 4 above; they will likely make this easier. The potentially harmful habit you are stopping is conflict.

If you are stumbling into some of these issues while planning your wedding, it's OK. This is not necessarily something that you missed. The legal aspect of marriage can sometimes add a little pressure to the relationship, uncovering insecurities or unintentional avoidance. Be intentional with the foundation you are creating during your engagement. Keep these five principles in mind, and remember that no one is perfect all the time.

item.title: Effective Leadership Is a Craft, Not a Checklist
item.description:
Leadership

Effective Leadership Is a Craft, Not a Checklist

Why context, not checklists, drives effective leadership.

Posted September 29, 2026

Key points
  • Memorizing leadership advice often misses the deeper thinking that drives genuine impact.
  • Before skilled leaders ask a powerful question, deliver difficult feedback, or build consensus, they work.
  • Effective leadership depends on context, not scripted checklists or catchy phrases.

Are your social media platforms flooded with attention-grabbing titles like:

  • “Top 10 Things Great Leaders Say”
  • “Five Phrases That Build Trust”
  • “Seven Ways to Give Better Feedback”

These lists signal a promise to distinguish exceptional leaders from average ones, packaged into language that is easy to consume, remember, and apply. They also offer scripts for difficult conversations, templates for influence, and formulas for sounding more confident or authoritative. Yet their popularity raises an important question:

Are these lists actually teaching us how to become better leaders? Or are they simply highlighting the visible outputs of the invisible work of leadership?

What if these lists are not actually teaching us how to be better leaders but are instead giving us a window into the hidden labor of leadership?

Autopilot Leadership Fails Without Context

Leadership is not defined by AI or the words spoken in a moment, but by the invisible work that precedes them. Before a skilled leader asks a powerful question, delivers difficult feedback, or builds consensus, they have often engaged in a complex series of cognitive and emotional tasks: regulating their own reactions, examining assumptions, considering multiple perspectives, anticipating consequences, assessing context, and reflecting on what another person may be experiencing. This invisible work rarely appears in a social media post because it is difficult to observe and even more difficult to teach. As a result, we risk confusing the performance of leadership with the practice of leadership.

One piece of leadership responsibility that we often see missing from those we coach, especially new leaders, is the understanding that they need to have time to think. When an effective leader comes to a conclusion or makes a statement, it rarely happens by chance. The leader has prepared for and contemplated how best to handle the issue at hand. For example, if you hear a leader ask a question like “Help me understand what’s driving this concern,” what you don’t hear is "I need to remain curious without putting someone on defense, I need to consider multiple perspectives, I need to choose inquiry over judgment, or I need to be sure not to simply react to what I hear, but to process it." These invisible components get lost when people use a script rather than strive to understand how to properly engage.

The work and behaviors of leaders shouldn’t just be reduced to these attention-grabbing checklists and scripts to follow. Effective leadership requires a much deeper level of understanding and reflection. Leaders must be able to:

  • Anticipate challenges before they arise
  • Thoughtfully process their experiences
  • Recognize the impact their words and actions have on others

An important phrase that every leader needs to remember is that every piece of leadership advice you are given "depends" on the context, from the context you were advised from and the context you are currently operating within. Leading means dealing with people, and with people comes complexity. Leaders need to continually examine and test their own assumptions while remaining curious about the assumptions and perspectives held by those around them. Research published in Management Review Quarterly and the Journal of Studies in Social Sciences and Humanities reminds us that reflective practice enables leaders to engage in both self-reflection and dialogue with others, while adaptive leadership emphasizes the importance of diagnosing situations, challenging assumptions, and responding to contextual realities. This kind of intentional thinking is what allows leaders to adapt their approach to the realities of each unique situation rather than relying on predetermined responses.

The danger of memorizing leadership advice without fully understanding it is that the invisible work of leadership can easily be disguised and, even worse, lost. Genuine leadership happens in the moments between the scripted conversations. It is in the ability to read a room, notice what is not being said, recognize underlying concerns, and respond with authenticity. When leaders focus too heavily on repeating the "right" phrases, interactions can begin to feel performative rather than meaningful. Employees are often quick to recognize the difference between a leader who is simply following a formula and one who is genuinely engaged, listening, and learning. It is these unseen elements of reflection, awareness, and adaptability that transform leadership from a performance into a purposeful relationship built on trust and credibility.

Learning Is Part of the Work Leaders Do

Cheat sheet checklists also point to the importance that processing levels have on our learning. First highlighted in 1976 in the British Journal of Educational Psychology, there is evidence that deep processing can help with learning. More recent research supports this, as it reveals that deep processing has significant advantages for learning and memory. So again, we caution against using these lists as a starting point for understanding concepts and note that one's processing level may also impede true learning and the ability to remember these concepts.

So, the next time a social media post offers "10 Things Great Leaders Say," look beyond the words themselves. The phrases are useful, but they are not the lesson. The real lesson is the invisible work that made those phrases effective. Great leaders are not created by memorized responses. They are distinguished by the thinking, reflection, and perspective-taking that happens before they speak.

item.title: The Lindsay Clancy Case and the Limits of Diagnosis
item.description:
Psychiatry

The Lindsay Clancy Case and the Limits of Diagnosis

Why mental health treatment requires more than a psychiatric diagnosis.

Posted September 29, 2026

Key points
  • Discourse has focused on the “right” diagnosis for Lindsay Clancy, as if that would've prevented the tragedy.
  • Effective mental health treatment may require both sustained psychotherapy and medication.
  • Psychodynamic therapy engages with the whole person, not just symptoms, and offers sustained healing.

The Lindsay Clancy case fascinates us as a society in part due to cultural splitting over motherhood, as I addressed in a previous post. But it’s also acting as a lightning rod for other issues.

A quick summary of the case: Lindsay Clancy admitted to strangling her three children before she threw herself out of her bedroom window in a suicide attempt that left her paralyzed from the waist down.

Beginning in September 2022, she was seen by at least six clinicians, treated with 14 medications, and sought help at clinics, ERs, and psychiatric hospitals, yet her symptoms became worse. Her legal defense claims she suffered from bipolar disorder and postpartum psychosis that, ultimately, led her to believe she heard a voice telling her to kill the children and herself.

While the cultural discourse is segmenting into two camps—Clancy as an evil mother or victim of mental illness—the case is also acting as a spotlight for another issue: How we have come as a culture to understand what constitutes effective mental health “treatment.” Her case highlights the difference between “psychiatric diagnosis” and a rarely used term, “psychotherapeutic diagnosis.”

The public discourse has focused on “What diagnosis did Clancy have?” For example, whether she was suffering from postpartum depression, postpartum psychosis, bipolar disorder, or some combination. It’s as if identifying her precise diagnosis—or diagnoses—could have definitively prevented the fatal outcome. This focus elevates the status of psychiatric diagnosis and assessment, asking them to explain, inform, and predict far more than they often can, while minimizing—or even eclipsing—questions about the actual service, care, and mental health treatment a person receives.

Was Clancy Really ‘In Treatment’?

Clancy had frequent appointments, numerous medication trials and adjustments, hospitalization, and acute treatment. Yet she also did not engage in the regular psychotherapy repeatedly recommended to her. Psychiatric nurse practitioner Rebecca Jollotta developed alternative treatment plans for Clancy that included behavioral therapy, support groups, and meditation. Clancy attended four sessions with a therapist before stopping.1

In addition, Clancy’s psychiatrist, Dr. Jennifer Tufts, repeatedly recommended that she engage in regular individual psychotherapy. Most importantly, during Tufts’ August 10, 2026 testimony, she repeatedly recommended individual therapy on a weekly basis.2 According to the Boston Globe’s live trial coverage, Tufts testified that Clancy only saw a therapist at Aster Mental Health twice.2

Clancy’s difficulties sustaining regular psychotherapy appointments are themselves clinically significant and, if understood and addressed, may have made a meaningful difference in her life.

While we have heard much about psychiatric diagnosis—postpartum psychosis, depression, bipolar disorder, and anxiety—what hasn’t emerged as strongly in the Clancy case is the psychotherapeutic assessment and diagnosis, including the need for regular, sustained, longer-term psychotherapeutic treatment when a patient is clearly struggling with multiple symptoms and issues. Research supports that integrated, combined treatment that includes both medication and psychotherapy is typically needed. A 2026 study concluded that combined treatment significantly outperforms pharmacotherapy alone, specifically across patients with severe psychiatric comorbidities, or in other words, patients suffering from multiple issues at once.3

Similarly, a JAMA Psychiatry study found that while antipsychotic medication is mandatory to treat the biological foundation of psychosis, medication alone does not resolve the secondary terror, trauma, and anxiety that symptoms, such as hallucinations, cause.4 Adding psychotherapy on top of medication produced statistically significant drops in anxiety-related distress and hallucination severity compared with medication alone.

What Psychodynamic Therapy Can Add

Psychotherapy is focused on different outcomes than medication management and supportive check-ins. For Clancy, the therapist would seek to understand her psychologically. How does she experience motherhood, herself, her children, dependency, aggression, separation? What are her relational patterns? What are her defenses?

When a patient is accompanied psychologically, they are more likely to heal. For Clancy, there is no public evidence that she was followed longitudinally by one psychotherapist who accompanied her throughout treatment and could track her feelings, thoughts, behaviors, and symptoms, and, importantly, changes in any of these over time. Tragically, the absence of such a relationship has become increasingly normalized in mental health care—a source of frustration and outrage for many patients and clinicians, while others may not even recognize what is missing and the clinical significance of its absence.

Perhaps part of the complexity is that psychiatric diagnosis, medications, and symptom management provide concrete frameworks for treatment but offer little guidance for the less tangible dimensions of care, particularly the sustained, attuned, psychotherapeutic relationship through which we come to know who a person is, how they are functioning, and what they are struggling with, so they may be treated effectively. This is where the Psychodynamic Diagnostic Manual (PDM) becomes relevant.

It assesses personality organization, mental functioning, relational patterns, affect regulation, defenses, subjective experience, and the meaning of symptoms. It offers a psychotherapeutic or psychodynamic diagnosis that considers what this individual can and cannot think about, feel, symbolize, and speak. It considers the meaning of her symptoms, understood through the larger context of her development, relational, and affective life. The PDM does not hold that psychiatric diagnosis is unimportant; rather, it contends that it may be necessary yet insufficient for understanding an individual, complex human being, which is often the focus of psychotherapy, especially psychodynamic therapy.

The PDM was developed to support a psychologically meaningful understanding of the patient, in a mental health system in which diagnostic classification has increasingly come to substitute for understanding the person. It does not replace but complements descriptive psychiatric diagnosis by considering the role of personality, mental functioning, relational patterns, and the individual’s subjective experience of symptoms.

Rather than asking, “what psychiatric disorder did Clancy have?” it asks, “who is Clancy psychologically, what was happening inside her as her mental health deteriorated?” These questions cannot be answered through a diagnosis. They typically require a sustained psychotherapeutic relationship in which the patient’s story–her inner, outer, and relational world–can become known.

In the Lindsay Clancy case, we cannot know her unconscious conflicts, personality organization, possible maternal ambivalence, and the meaning of her symptoms through the records and media, which is perhaps part of our fascination with her case—she raises numerous questions and provides few answers.

item.title: How to Handle Life's Unexpected Curveballs
item.description:
Stress

How to Handle Life's Unexpected Curveballs

Mind-body strategies for calming the stress alarm.

Posted September 29, 2026

Key points
  • Our stress response is similar to a smoke alarm: It can sound whether there's an actual fire or burning toast.
  • Recognizing the physical, emotional, cognitive, and behavioral components of stress can help to manage it.
  • Specific strategies can help calm physical sensations, emotions, thoughts, and behaviors of stress.
Source: Neon Pixels Studio/Pixabay

We got a deluge of rain in this recent Nor’easter here in Massachusetts. In my haste to prepare for possible large wind gusts, I pulled the umbrella out of our glass table on the concrete deck in our backyard, as I often do…except this time, as I pulled it out, I was startled when the glass instantly shattered into literally thousands of pieces. What was once a large table that seated eight was now a pile of shards scattered far and wide. Here I was with dangerous glass all over, a torrential tropical storm coming any moment to carry the glass far and wide, and a packed day of patients.

I’ll be the first to admit I don’t always handle these unexpected curveballs as well as I’d like, though over time I’ve discovered some things that help.

While stress can often feel like one single overwhelming experience, one of the things I’ve found helpful over the years is to understand our stress response as having four interconnected responses: what’s happening in the body and what’s happening with our emotions, our thoughts, and our behaviors. Each influences the others, and each can be met with specific strategies to help dial down the brain’s alarm system.

Understanding Our Stress Response

First, it can be helpful to understand that our nervous system and brain are always working together below the surface of our awareness to assess for threat and safety. It’s a kind of threat detection system similar to the smoke alarms in our homes, and it works on a better-safe-than-sorry method. If a threat is detected, the alarm sounds automatically. It doesn’t matter whether it is a true life-threatening fire or just the toast burning in the toaster; the alarm doesn’t differentiate. Our brains respond similarly to “threats”—whether saber-tooth tigers or traffic jams or arguments or getting up to speak in front of a large audience. This makes sense from an evolutionary perspective to have an alarm that sounds quickly and indiscriminately. If it looks like a saber-tooth tiger, better fight or flee; don’t stick around to ponder if perhaps it’s just something else rustling in the grass.

The brain and autonomic nervous system are constantly trying to determine what resources are needed in any given moment to meet the current situation at hand. When threats or dangers are detected, the protection circuits of our sympathetic nervous system (designed to fight or flee) are activated. We get a jolt of energy to mobilize, or our system goes into shutdown if things feel too overwhelming (with the help of the dorsal branch of our vagus nerve). Alternatively, if safety is detected, resources can be allocated toward biological rest, growth, and recovery through the ventral vagal pathways of our parasympathetic nervous system. We feel calm, connected, and balanced.

So going back to the shattered table scenario, this mishap is immediately read as a threat, and my stress response becomes activated:

Physically, my heart starts pumping faster to get blood to my fighting muscles. Stress chemicals are released into my bloodstream to help me prepare to fight or flee.

Emotionally, I feel a shift from my nice, peaceful mood of enjoying the afternoon to frustration, anger, worry (how will I possibly clean all this up before the storm?), and overwhelm (I have meetings and patients and don’t have time to work and attend to this mess).

Mentally, my mind starts creating a narrative about what just happened, and it also starts projecting a narrative of what is to come (if only I hadn’t done this, I’m so stupid for being careless, I won’t be able to clean this all up and then people will get hurt…).

Behaviorally, I am making choices about how I react in the next moments (do I yell and swear, curl up in a ball, spring into action?).

My stress response can at times give me a helpful jolt of energy to mobilize, but if I am overtaken by stress, I lose access to all the inner resources that are available when my nervous system is in balance (e.g., perspective taking, problem-solving, clarity, self-compassion, creativity, curiosity, patience, etc.). The stress I’m feeling is understandable, but if the alarm continues to blast, I’m not able to respond most effectively.

Calming the Alarm and Bringing Balance Back Into the Nervous System

One way to think about responding to our built-in threat detection system is to intentionally introduce cues of safety to help calm the alarm. First, we notice that the alarm is sounding. Then, we choose strategies to soothe each of these four areas: our body, our emotions, our mental activity, and our behaviors.

Here are some examples of strategies to address each of these four dimensions of the stress response:

Calming the body: Take long, slow exhalations; feel your feet on the ground and notice your senses (what you can see, hear, touch, taste, or smell); take deep, long sighs; cross your arms across your chest and tap back and forth on each shoulder like a butterfly tapping its wings.

Tending to emotions: Mindfully notice and name what emotions are present; tell yourself “all my emotions are welcome here” and make space for them to be rather than try to push them away; put a hand on your heart and imagine sending care to any parts of you that are struggling; call to mind supportive people (or spiritual figures, pets, or even favorite places in nature) and let yourself feel immersed in their caring energy.

Loosening the grip of thoughts: Speak to yourself in the third person to get some distance ("I can see Beth is having a hard time right now, thinking she can’t handle this"); notice any charged thoughts you are having and add the phrase “I notice I’m having the thought that…” (e.g., instead of "I’m so stupid for being careless," say to yourself, “I notice I’m having the thought that I’m so stupid for being careless). This helps to create a bit of space between you and your thoughts, to loosen their grip.

Choosing behaviors skillfully: Connect with your deepest values. Ask questions such as “What is most important to me about how I respond?” “How do I want to show up for others and myself?” “What inner qualities do I most want to harness right now?” “How can I take care of myself going into the next moments of the day?” “What would my wisest self do right now?”

We can learn, practice, and rehearse these strategies during calmer times so that when the curveballs come at us, we are familiar with what to do. As I look at the now empty table frame where the glass once was, I am reminded of how suddenly stressful situations can descend upon us, and how each becomes an opportunity to build resilience as we learn to quiet the alarm. And there’s always next year for that new table.
